# kernl

> Full text of every page on this site, in reading order.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/index.md -->

# Run things you don't have to trust.

> kernl is a shell that runs small applets in a sealed sandbox. Your identity, contacts, messages and files stay yours; applets borrow them only while you watch.

kernl runs small, self-contained applets in a sealed sandbox. **Your identity, contacts, messages and files are yours** and travel with you. An applet borrows them only with your say-so, and only while you watch.

Pass, slow down, or cut off. Each line is a decision you can see.

## A window, a loan, and a line it cannot cross alone.

*Sealed*

### A window of its own

Each applet runs in a sealed frame with no address of its own and no way to call out. It can draw and compute; it cannot reach anything you did not hand it.

*Borrowed*

### Your things, on loan

Contacts, messages, files and your account are read by the shell on the applet's behalf. A grant is something you gave and can take back, and the shell shows what each one changes.

*Watched*

### A network it reaches through you

Everything an applet sends or fetches goes through the guard. You can see it, slow it down, or cut it off, per applet, at any time.

## kernl is opinionated so you don't have to be.

It is built on [kehto](https://github.com/kehto/web), an open toolkit that leaves every choice open. kernl makes the choices, in your favour, and writes down why.

1. **Everything in one place, reached one way**
   One store, one connection, one account manager. There is no second copy of your world for an applet to get at.
2. **The shell empowers you and contains the applet**
   Those are its only two jobs, in that order.
3. **Protections are on by default**
   You loosen them per applet. A developer flag never can.
4. **One account, many networks, no brand names**
   Downloads, sharing and mail plug in as bridges named by what they do for you.
5. **No private-messaging system is "the best"**
   The shell describes each provider truthfully and lets you choose the one your correspondent can read.

[Read the five opinions](https://kernlize.github.io/why/)

## Alpha, and said so.

kernl is alpha software. The sandbox, the guard and private messaging work today. Bridges for downloads, sharing and mail have their contracts in place and wait for backends; the shell shows them as unavailable rather than pretending.

Applets are verified by content hash before they run and re-checked on every read from cache. If the bytes change, the applet's grants die with them.

[Build on it](https://kernlize.github.io/developers/) [Read the decisions](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions)

## Free. $0, no tier, no catch.

*Price*

### $0

No subscription and no paid features. The whole shell is the free version.

*Licence*

### MIT

Read it, fork it, run your own copy. The source is public and so are the decisions behind it.

*To try it*

### No sign-up

[Open the preview](https://kernlize.github.io/app/?preview=1) and use the shell with sample applets, entirely in your browser.

## Asked often, answered plainly.

### What is an applet?

A small, self-contained program published as a single verified file. kernl checks its content hash before it runs and gives it a sealed window with no network of its own.

### What can an applet see?

Only what you grant, for as long as you grant it. By default it sees your theme, its own storage and which account is signed in. Network access, messages, notifications and files are each a separate grant you can take back.

### Does kernl hold my keys?

No applet ever does. You can sign in with a browser extension or a remote signer so your key never enters the shell, or create a local account whose key is encrypted with a password you choose.

### What does kernl cost?

Nothing. kernl is free and open source under the MIT licence. There is no account to buy and no paid tier.

### Can I try it without signing in?

Yes. The preview runs the whole shell in your browser with sample applets and a throwaway account. Nothing leaves the tab.

### Is it ready for daily use?

Not yet. kernl is alpha software. The sandbox, the guard and private messaging work; downloads, sharing and mail are waiting for their backends, and the shell says so.

# Five opinions, held on your behalf.

> The five opinions behind kernl, in plain words: one place for your things, a shell that contains applets, protections on by default, many networks, no ranking.

kernl is built on [kehto](https://github.com/kehto/web), a toolkit that deliberately decides nothing. kernl decides everything kehto left open, and every decision breaks the same way: **towards the person at the keyboard**.

01

## Everything in one place, reached one way.

Your messages, contacts, files and account live in one store inside the shell, read through one connection and signed by one account manager. kernl does not hedge that with a second library doing the same job, because every extra copy is another thing to protect.

- Applets never get a handle on the store. Services read from it for them.
- Your keys are never raw bytes outside the signer that holds them.
- One path in and out means one place to watch.

02

## The shell exists to empower you and to contain the applet.

A shell has two jobs. It gives you a place where your identity and your things are yours and portable. And it gives an untrusted program a place to run where the worst it can do is bounded. kernl cannot protect you from everything. It does all of it that it can.

- Applets run in a sealed frame with no network of their own.
- They never hold keys and never see text you did not ask to show them.
- Every write the shell makes for an applet is shown to you as what it changes, not as code.
- An applet's identity is bound to the exact bytes you verified. Changed bytes are a new applet, with no grants.

03

## Protections are on by default. You loosen them, not the developer.

When the toolkit offers a privacy or safety mitigation, kernl turns it on, in its strict setting, and documents how to ease it. You matter more than the applet developer does. Within reason: an applet interface so tight that nothing can be written protects nobody.

- The [guard](https://kernlize.github.io/guard/) ships strict, with focus-aware tightening.
- Hidden and minimised applets have their traffic deferred.
- A protection is loosened per applet, by you. Never globally, never by a flag.

04

## One account, many networks, no brand names.

Your account is how you are known, how applets are found and verified, and how you reach other people. It is not the only network kernl speaks. Downloads, sharing and mail plug in as [bridges](https://kernlize.github.io/bridges/), behind the same consent and quota rules as everything else.

- Bridges are named by what they do for you, not by the wire format they speak.
- This site does not name protocols. The protocol is the plumbing. The person is the point.

05

## No private-messaging system is "the best".

kernl supports any reasonable private-messaging provider through one interface. You pick the one your correspondent can read, and the shell makes that choice visible and reversible.

- The shell does not rank providers. It [describes them](https://kernlize.github.io/messaging/): forward secrecy or not, what the network can see, whether the other person needs the same app.
- Applets see one messaging surface that spans every provider you enabled.

## The tie-breakers, in order.

1. **Your safety and agency**
   Always first.
2. **Doing what the open format actually says**
   Conformance with the upstream specification, not a convenient reading of it.
3. **The applet developer's ability to build**
   A competent developer, reading the docs, must still have a clear path.
4. **Documentation accuracy**
   A feature without docs is not shipped.
5. **Performance, then code size**
   In that order, and last.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/guard/index.md -->

# Everything between an applet and the world.

> What the kernl guard does between an applet and your network: a sealed sandbox, verified bytes, budgets, flood control and a question before anything destructive is signed, loosened only by you.

The guard is the set of protections that sit between an applet and you. It is **on from the first second**, in its strict setting. It tells you when it acts and why, and only you can loosen it.

## Eleven protections, in plain words.

1. **A sealed sandbox**
   Each applet runs in a frame with no address of its own and a policy that forbids every network call. The only way out is through the shell.
2. **Identity bound to the bytes, with revocation**
   An applet's identity is tied to the exact code you verified and to the live connection it runs over. If either changes, the connection is cut and the frame is removed. What you allowed stays with that exact code, so it applies again when you reopen it.
3. **Verified before it runs, re-checked from cache**
   Applet code is checked against its content hash before the first run. Cached copies are checked again on every read, so a tampered cache cannot slip past.
4. **Replay detection**
   A message the shell has already handled is not handled twice, and a message meant for one window cannot be replayed into another.
5. **Behavioural rate limits**
   Each kind of request has its own budget per applet. A request over budget is refused before the shell acts on it.
6. **Focus-aware tightening**
   An applet you are not looking at is measured against a smaller budget, and the guard tells you when it goes over. Going over is reported, not refused; the budget above still applies. The shell decides what is focused; the applet is never asked.
7. **Hidden applets that keep downloading are stopped**
   While an applet is minimised or hidden, the shell counts its downloads. One that goes past its allowance is quarantined: the shell closes it and tells you. Its other requests are recorded, not held back.
8. **Flood control and quarantine**
   The shell counts every message an applet sends. Bursts above the per-second rate are reported to you. One that keeps flooding is quarantined: its connection is cut and its window closed, and you can open it again when you choose.
9. **Size caps**
   Requests for files and long-running searches are measured against a maximum size. An oversized one is reported to you; it is not stopped, because the shell measures it after it has been handled.
10. **Device permissions denied**
    Camera, microphone, location and the rest are off for every applet. There is no prompt to be tricked into.
11. **Consent for destructive changes**
    Before an applet changes your profile, who you follow, your connections or one of your lists, or deletes something you posted, the shell shows you what would change and waits for your answer. If you say no, nothing is signed. Everyday posts go through without a question, and the shell asks again every time.

*What you see*

## Every refusal has a reason.

The guard records an event for every request it refuses, holds, reports or stops, with a stable reason you can read. Nothing is silently dropped.

*Loosening it*

## By you, and only you.

Three profiles exist: strict, balanced and relaxed. The shell boots strict, every time. For now the choice applies to the whole shell and is forgotten when you reload; easing one applet at a time is planned. No configuration file or developer flag can ease the guard. The [documentation](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/) lists each limit by profile.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/messaging/index.md -->

# Described, not ranked.

> kernl supports several private-message providers and ranks none. Each is described by what it protects: forward secrecy, metadata, groups, what the other needs.

Private messaging in kernl works across several providers. **None of them is "the best".** The shell tells you plainly what each one protects, and you pick the one the person you are writing to can read.

## The same six questions, asked of each.

### Private messages

The default. Each message is wrapped so the network cannot see who wrote it or what it says.

- **Forward secrecy**: No
- **Heals after a key leak**: No
- **Metadata protection**: Partial
- **Other person needs this app**: No
- **Groups**: Yes
- **Experimental**: No

### Legacy messages

The original format, kept so old conversations still open. The content is hidden; who talks to whom and when is not.

- **Forward secrecy**: No
- **Heals after a key leak**: No
- **Metadata protection**: None
- **Other person needs this app**: No
- **Groups**: No
- **Experimental**: No

### Ratchet sessions

Keys change with every message, so a leak today does not expose yesterday. Both sides need an app that speaks it.

- **Forward secrecy**: Yes
- **Heals after a key leak**: Yes
- **Metadata protection**: Partial
- **Other person needs this app**: Yes
- **Groups**: No
- **Experimental**: Yes

## What the rows mean.

- **Forward secrecy**: If your keys leak today, messages from before today stay unreadable.
- **Heals after a key leak**: Once both of you keep writing, a leaked key stops being useful to whoever has it.
- **Metadata protection**: How much someone watching the network learns about who talks to whom and when. "Partial" means the sender and timing are hidden but delivery is not.
- **Other person needs this app**: Whether your correspondent must use an app that speaks the same provider.
- **Experimental**: The provider is still changing and may lose history between versions. kernl says so before you enable it.

Applets see one messaging surface that spans every provider you enabled. The choice of provider stays with you, is shown on every conversation, and can be changed. More in the [documentation](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/).

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/bridges/index.md -->

# Named by what they do for you.

> Bridges let kernl reach other networks for you. Web fetch works today; downloads, sharing and mail have their contracts in place and wait for their backends.

A bridge is a service the shell owns that turns a link into bytes or a conversation on another network. Every bridge sits behind **the same consent and quota rules** as everything else an applet can ask for.

## What works today, and what is waiting.

*Works today*

### Web fetch

Fetches a web address for an applet, through the shell, with a policy that refuses private and local addresses so an applet cannot use you to look inside your own network.

*Needs a backend*

### Downloads

Understands the links people already share for large files and newsgroup posts. The parsing and the contract exist; the part that actually moves bytes does not yet.

*Needs a backend*

### Sharing

Person-to-person file sharing between people who choose each other. Same story: the contract is in place and tested, the backend is on the roadmap.

*Needs a backend*

### Mail

Turns a mail link into a conversation. The locator is parsed and the contract is defined; sending and receiving wait for a backend you would run or trust.

A bridge without a backend reports itself as unavailable, and the shell shows exactly that. It will not pretend, and an applet cannot tell the difference between "unavailable" and "you said no".

## Every bridge, the same way.

1. **An applet asks; the shell resolves**
   The applet never touches the other network. It hands the shell a link and gets back bytes or a conversation, or a reason.
2. **You see the request**
   Each request shows up in the [guard](https://kernlize.github.io/guard/) with what it is for, and counts against the applet's budget.
3. **Named for people**
   "Downloads", "sharing", "mail". Not the name of the wire format underneath. If you care which one it is, the documentation says.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/developers/index.md -->

# Build something people can run without trusting you.

> How to build for kernl: write an applet in the open applet format, learn what the sealed sandbox and strict guard mean for your code, and read the docs first.

An applet for kernl is a small, self-contained web page in the open applet format. It gets a sealed window, asks for what it needs, and reaches the world through the shell. **That constraint is the feature.**

## Three places to read.

*Docs*

### [kernl documentation](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/)

Concepts, how-tos and the reference for every package: the guard and its profiles, messaging providers, bridges and the shell's composition root.

*Toolkit*

### [kehto](https://github.com/kehto/web)

The open, unopinionated toolkit kernl is built on. If you want to build a different shell with different opinions, start there.

*Format*

### [The applet format's site](https://napplet.run/)

How applets are packaged, addressed and verified, and the message domains an applet can ask a shell for. kernl hosts this format without changing it.

## What your applet gets, and does not.

1. **A sealed window**
   Your code runs in a frame with no origin and a policy that blocks every direct network call. Draw, compute, and talk to the shell over its message port.
2. **Grants, not permissions**
   Ask for the domains you need. The shell narrows what it advertises to what the user has granted, shows every write as what it changes, and lets the user take a grant back.
3. **The strict profile**
   Rate limits, size caps, hidden-window deferral and focus-aware tightening are on. Design for them: batch requests, do less when hidden, and expect a refusal to carry a stable reason you can show.
4. **Verified bytes**
   Your applet is identified by the hash of its content. Ship a new version and it is a new identity with fresh grants. That is deliberate.
5. **Messaging across providers**
   One messaging surface spans every provider the user enabled. You do not pick the provider; the user does, and your applet works either way.

*Source*

## MIT, opening after alpha.

Four small packages and one app. Behaviour is specified in scenarios before it is implemented, and coverage is complete. Decisions, and the reasons for them, are written down and published now. The source itself is private during alpha and opens under the MIT licence with the first public release.

[Read the decisions](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions)

*For agents*

## Read this site as text.

Every page has a Markdown twin at `index.md` next to it, listed in [llms.txt](https://kernlize.github.io/llms.txt). The full text is in [llms-full.txt](https://kernlize.github.io/llms-full.txt), and the docs publish their own.

# kernl shell

> The kernl shell. Open an applet by its address and run it in a sealed sandbox, with your identity, contacts and messages on loan only while you watch.
